questions.title: Import data with the correct types
questions.prompt: Import the film-permit workbook. How many data records and columns are there? Explain why date/time fields must be recognised as dates, not text.
questions.answer: 33,502 records and 14 columns, excluding the header. StartDateTime, EndDateTime and EnteredOn must retain date/time meaning; numeric date arithmetic on text is unreliable. In a text import, explicitly select the correct delimiter and date/number locale.
questions.hint: Do not count the header. Check StartDateTime after import.

questions.title: Filter and count permits
questions.prompt: How many Shooting Permit records are in Brooklyn? Show an Excel method, not just a number.
questions.answer: 10,367. One method is COUNTIFS with EventType="Shooting Permit" and Borough="Brooklyn". A filtered pivot table counting EventID also works. Count permits, not unique dates.
questions.hint: Apply both criteria at the same time.
checks: Keep the formula or pivot table visible

questions.title: Calculate permit duration in hours
questions.prompt: Find the mean permit duration in hours for Shooting Permit records. Give the unrounded mean to two decimals and explain the Excel conversion.
questions.answer: 16.98 hours. In a helper column use =(EndDateTime-StartDateTime)*24; Excel date differences are days. Filter EventType="Shooting Permit", then average the helper. Do not average only Brooklyn for this question.
questions.hint: Excel date differences are measured in days.

questions.title: Count missing ZIP codes
questions.prompt: How many permit records have a missing ZIP code? Inspect the column and explain how the source represents missing values.
questions.answer: The source contains 11 missing ZIP codes recorded as the text N/A. Filter ZipCode to N/A or use COUNTIF on that marker. COUNTBLANK would skip those text values.
questions.hint: Look for a text placeholder as well as empty cells.

questions.title: Find the earliest and latest entry times
questions.prompt: Give the oldest and newest EnteredOn timestamps. Include the date and time.
questions.answer: Earliest 2011-12-07 16:38. Latest 2018-02-09 12:46. MIN and MAX work on the imported date/time field.
questions.hint: Use EnteredOn and format the results to include time.

questions.title: Find the most common shooting-permit category
questions.prompt: Among Shooting Permit records, find the category with the most records and give its count.
questions.answer: Television, with 16,731 records. Filter EventType to Shooting Permit, then count EventID by Category and sort descending.
questions.hint: Apply the event-type filter before grouping.

questions.title: Build a location and plant key
questions.prompt: Using the Case 2 source sheet, derive a location and plant key such as USA-12. Explain why PlantID by itself can repeat across locations.
questions.answer: For JAP1080-19M, the key is JAP-19. Use LEFT(A2,3) for the location and MID(A2,FIND("-",A2)+1,2) for the two-digit plant. Join them with a hyphen and fill down. A plant number can recur in different countries.
questions.hint: Combine the country code and the plant number, leaving out the pay-period letter.
checks: Keep both parts of the key

questions.title: Resolve data quality issues
questions.prompt: Identify four data-quality problems in the balance-sheet CSV and explain what you would do before analysis.
questions.answer: Examples: inconsistent missing inventories (blank, spaces, hyphens); inconsistent ticker spacing; duplicated APVO 2018 record; K/M suffixes; parentheses for negative depreciation; an unquoted comma inside Apple, Inc. disrupts CSV columns. Standardise missing values without replacing unknowns with zero, normalise identifiers, investigate duplicates, and parse units/signs. Do not guess the units of Total Current Assets from its magnitude: obtain metadata.
questions.hint: Look at identifiers, missing markers, units, duplicate records and CSV delimiters.
checks: Do not invent Total Current Assets units

questions.title: Join journal data
questions.prompt: Explain how to add BusinessUnit and account information to every journal line without dropping journal lines. Which identifiers should be used?
questions.answer: Use BusinessUnitID to match BusinessUnits and GLAccountNumber to match ChartOfAccounts. Use a lookup or left join from JELineItems. Preserve each journal line, flag unmatched IDs, and check that reference keys are unique so joins cannot multiply rows. A JENumber can occur on multiple journal lines; it is not a unique line identifier by itself.
questions.hint: Start with the journal lines as the table you must preserve.
checks: Check duplicate and unmatched reference keys
Do not assume JENumber is unique per line

questions.title: Preserve an audit trail
questions.prompt: Why should the repeatable journal-data solution retain formulas rather than replace all outputs with pasted values?
questions.answer: Formulas retain the mapping logic and dependencies, making the transformation easier to review and repeat on a consistently structured replacement dataset. Keep source worksheets intact, populate the requested solution columns, and test both successful matches and unmatched IDs. A pasted number alone does not show how it was derived.
questions.hint: Think about review, re-performance and future refreshes.

questions.title: Compare two payroll systems
questions.prompt: Compare total gross wages in the supplied 2015 and 2016 extracts. Define the measure consistently, and compute 2016 minus 2015.
questions.answer: 2015 gross wages: 1,086,734.19; 2016: 1,352,789.75; increase: 266,055.56. 2015 uses Reg_Pay + OT_Pay; 2016 uses Gross_Wages. Do not add overtime twice in 2016. Both extracts cover the first six months; row counts and aggregation levels differ. Keep all supplied rows for these totals.
questions.hint: Gross_Wages already includes overtime in 2016.

questions.title: Investigate missing employee numbers
questions.prompt: How many 2016 rows have a missing Employee_Number, and what total Gross_Wages do those rows contain? What can you conclude?
questions.answer: 68 rows, with total gross wages 32,951.29. These are data-quality exceptions requiring follow-up. The extract alone does not establish fraud or prove that an employee does not exist. Employee_ID is a separate field and is not the requested Employee_Number.
questions.hint: Test Employee_Number, not Employee_ID or Employee_Name.
checks: Separate an exception from proof of fraud

questions.title: Compare average gross pay per hour
questions.prompt: Calculate company-wide gross pay per hour for each extract, including overtime. Explain why an average of individual row rates can differ.
questions.answer: 2015: USD 33.05 using 32,878.75 hours. 2016: USD 33.20 using 40,742.40 hours. Divide total pay by total hours, which weights the result by hours.
questions.hint: Sum regular and overtime hours for each year and use the corresponding gross-wage total.

questions.title: Estimate January 2016 payroll from the 2015 pattern
questions.prompt: Use January’s share of the first six months of 2015 gross wages to estimate January 2016 gross wages from the 2016 six-month total.
questions.answer: January 2015 gross pay is USD 178,365.77, or 16.41% of the six-month total. Applying the share at full precision gives estimated January 2016 gross pay of USD 222,033.49. This assumes the monthly pattern carries over.
questions.hint: Divide January 2015 gross pay by the 2015 six-month gross pay first.
checks: Apply the share to 2016 gross pay

questions.title: Predict sales
questions.prompt: Using the temperature model, predict daily sales when tmax is 70°F. Give dollars to two decimals.
questions.answer: 3255.87. Prediction = intercept + temperature coefficient × 70. Include the intercept. This is a fitted conditional mean, not a guaranteed outcome.
questions.hint: Do not omit the intercept.

questions.title: Interpret the temperature coefficient
questions.prompt: Interpret the temperature coefficient. What change does the model predict for a 10°F increase? Does this demonstrate causality?
questions.answer: The model associates a 1°F increase with 7.579688 additional dollars of predicted daily sales. A 10°F increase corresponds to 75.80. Observational association alone does not establish causality; season, holidays and other omitted factors may matter.
questions.hint: Multiply the slope by 10.

questions.title: Assess statistical evidence
questions.prompt: Using the reported p-value, assess the temperature slope at the 5% level. What does R² tell you, and what does it not tell you?
questions.answer: The temperature p-value is 0.00766585; compare it with 0.05. The slope is statistically significant under the OLS assumptions. R²=0.0227 describes in-sample explained variation, not causal proof, a guarantee of forecast accuracy, or the probability the model is true.
questions.hint: Statistical significance and practical forecasting usefulness are different.
checks: Do not claim causality or certain forecasts

questions.title: Compare game-day predictions
questions.prompt: In the interaction model, let L=5000. Find predicted sales without a game and with a game, then the difference. For the numeric check, enter only the difference in dollars.
questions.answer: No game: 4142.39. Game: 4583.12. Difference = b_G + b_LG × 5000 = 440.73. It is not just the game coefficient.
questions.hint: Switching G from 0 to 1 changes the G term and L×G term.
checks: Interpret model comparison, not a proven causal effect

questions.title: Calculate the game-day slope
questions.prompt: What is the slope on L for game days? Explain how it differs from the slope on non-game days. Enter the game-day slope for the numeric check.
questions.answer: Non-game slope: 0.619594460. Game-day slope: b_L + b_LG = 0.630334132. The interaction changes how current predicted sales relate to sales 364 days earlier. L is a sales amount, not elapsed days.
questions.hint: Collect the terms multiplying L when G=1.

questions.title: Forecast seven days ahead
questions.prompt: Bob wants a sales forecast seven days after the last observed date. Explain what additional predictor information and validation you need before using these models for that forecast.
questions.answer: Identify the future target date. For the interaction model, obtain sales 364 days before that target date and the scheduled game-day status. For the temperature model, obtain a forecast of tmax, not the realised future weather. Evaluate predictions on a chronological holdout and communicate forecast uncertainty. In-sample fit alone is insufficient. The case workbook does not justify inventing missing future inputs.
questions.hint: Which values must be known at the time the forecast is made?

questions.title: Compare predictions at two temperatures
questions.prompt: Using the temperature model, calculate the change in predicted daily sales when tmax rises from 60°F to 80°F. Enter the dollar difference to two decimals.
questions.answer: 151.59. The intercept cancels, leaving the slope multiplied by 20°F.
questions.hint: Subtract the prediction at 60°F from the prediction at 80°F.

questions.title: Read the game-day coefficient
questions.prompt: In the interaction model, what comparison does the coefficient on G represent? Explain how to estimate the game-day difference at a realistic value of L.
questions.answer: The coefficient on G is the predicted difference when L=0. At a specified L, the difference is b_G + b_LG × L. Assess that combined effect at a value of L relevant to the question.
questions.hint: Set G to 0 and 1 while holding L constant.

questions.title: Explain the intercept and extrapolation
questions.prompt: In the temperature model, explain the intercept. Is a prediction at tmax=0°F supported by the observed temperature range?
questions.answer: The intercept is predicted daily sales at 0°F. The observed daily highs range from 28.94°F to 104°F, so 0°F requires extrapolation. The algebra still produces a number, but the sample provides limited evidence for that prediction.
questions.hint: Compare 0°F with the range shown under the model.

questions.title: Measure a change in prior sales on game days
questions.prompt: For a game day, calculate how much predicted sales change when L increases by $1,000. Report the change in dollars to two decimals.
questions.answer: 630.33. Multiply the game-day slope b_L + b_LG by 1,000.
questions.hint: Combine the terms that multiply L when G=1.

questions.title: Predict a non-game day
questions.prompt: Use the interaction model to predict sales on a non-game day with L equal to $4,000. Give your answer in dollars to two decimals.
questions.answer: 3522.79. Set G=0, which removes both G terms. Add the intercept to b_L × 4,000.
questions.hint: Both the game-day term and the interaction vanish when G=0.

questions.title: Design a fair forecast comparison
questions.prompt: How would you use the restaurant sales dates to compare the temperature and interaction models on forecast accuracy? Give one error measure and explain the split.
questions.answer: Use an earlier training window and a later common test window, or rolling-origin evaluation. Fit both models on the same training dates, predict the same later dates using inputs available when each forecast was made, and compare mean absolute error in dollars.
questions.hint: Think about which dates would have been in the past when a prediction was made.
checks: Compare predictions on the same dates
Choose and explain an error measure
Use only information available at forecast time

questions.title: Forecast seven days ahead using prior sales
questions.prompt: Use the prior-sales regression to forecast sales on 2019-01-07. The 7-day, 28-day and 364-day inputs in dollars are 3,252.00, 1,987.00 and 2,841.00, respectively. Give your result to two decimals.
questions.answer: USD 2,685.62. Use the intercept and multiply each prior sales amount by its matching coefficient. The input dates are 2018-12-31, 2018-12-10, 2018-01-08.
questions.hint: Match the 7-, 28- and 364-day coefficients to their own inputs.
checks: Match each lag to its own sales amount

questions.title: Interpret a squared temperature term
questions.prompt: Use the model with tmax and tmax squared. Is the fitted curve concave or convex? Can its temperature effect be represented by one constant slope?
questions.answer: The squared term is -0.410749, so the fitted curve is concave. The local slope changes with temperature and equals b₁ + 2 × b₂ × tmax. Interpret this association within the observed range.
questions.hint: Look at the sign on tmax squared.
checks: Use the sign of the squared term
Explain that the slope depends on temperature
Treat the relationship as an association

questions.title: Compare sales on game and non-game days
questions.prompt: Use the game-day model to find the predicted dollar difference between a game day and a non-game day. Give the difference to two decimals and explain what it measures.
questions.answer: USD 1,436.30. Changing G from 0 to 1 adds the G coefficient. This is an unadjusted difference between the groups. Other differences, including day of week, may explain part of it.
questions.hint: Set G to 1 and 0, then subtract.
checks: Report the G coefficient in dollars

questions.title: Compare the prior-sales slope on home-game days
questions.prompt: In the home-game model, calculate the slope on L for home games. Give the slope to four decimal places and explain how it differs from the slope on days without a home game.
questions.answer: On days without a home game the slope is 0.619049. On home-game days it is -0.040484, found by adding the interaction coefficient -0.659533. The comparison describes the fitted association.
questions.hint: Collect the coefficients multiplying L when H=1.
checks: Add the main and interaction slopes
Distinguish home games from all games

modelMethod: Aggregate sales and lagged sales fields by date, join to weather, and code dates absent from the football schedule as non-game days. The six models use the same 312 observed sales dates, OLS with intercept, and conventional homoskedastic standard errors. Forecast accuracy has not been measured on held-out dates.
